cards.title: SETH hardness of factor-two Closest Pair
cards.formal: The source asks whether SETH can imply a superlinear time lower bound for factor-two approximation of the monochromatic Closest Pair problem: for some constant ε>0, rule out algorithms running in O(n^{1+ε}) time on n points in dimension d=ω(log n). A factor-two algorithm must return two distinct input points whose distance is at most twice the minimum distance between any distinct input pair. The “2” denotes the approximation factor, not the Euclidean norm. The source permits “any metric” without fixing its computational representation or the full dimension regime, so this is not yet a fully specified conditional proposition.
cards.why: The factor-two threshold tests whether known fine-grained geometric hardness extends beyond the range accessible to existing reductions. Its significance is computational hardness at a fixed approximation endpoint, which requires a representation and dimension regime where the bound is not explained just by input length.
cards.status_note: Checked the source and its full preprint, the earlier theorem including its distance gap, and later-result searches through 12 September 2026. The exact factor-two target was not found resolved, but “any metric” and the dimension/representation-cost scope remain insufficiently specified for a complete benchmark statement. The 2023 result was checked at publisher-abstract level.

cards.review_note: The source asks for hardness in “any metric” but does not fix an eligible metric family or say precisely whether a witness metric or a universal result is intended. A metric distance oracle, a distance matrix, and explicitly encoded vectors are different computational inputs. It also gives only d=ω(log n), without an upper dimension/coordinate-bit regime or an n,d running-time convention, so a purported n^{1+ε} lower bound can otherwise be an input-reading artifact. Finally the algorithm’s randomness and the matching deterministic versus randomized SETH hypothesis must be selected. These choices are not supplied by the question or the checked full version; no particular norm, subpolynomial dimension bound or stronger hypothesis is silently substituted.

sentences: The question concerns returning a pair within factor two of the closest distance in one point set.
It asks whether SETH can rule out some n^{1+ε}-time algorithm in dimensions above logarithmic.
Known ℓ∞ hardness below factor two does not settle the closed factor-two guarantee.
The source’s triangle-inequality discussion is a limitation of certain reductions rather than a general impossibility theorem.
The card recovers these distinctions but still needs a metric, representation, dimension-cost regime and randomness convention.

cards.definitions: A metric space (M,dist) has dist:M×M→ℝ≥0, with dist(x,y)=0 iff x=y, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. For a finite set P={p₁,…,pₙ} of n≥2 distinct points, let OPT(P)=min_{1≤i<j≤n}dist(pᵢ,pⱼ). A factor-two Closest Pair output is an index pair i<j with dist(pᵢ,pⱼ)≤2OPT(P). This is monochromatic: there is a single point set, and no red/blue constraint on the returned pair. The source studies vector spaces with distances ℓ_p(x,y)=(Σ_j|x_j−y_j|^p)^{1/p} for fixed p≥1, Hamming distance counting unequal coordinates, and in related work ℓ∞(x,y)=max_j|x_j−y_j|. The open question does not choose one of these metrics or limit “any metric” to this list. For a dimension function d(n), d=ω(log n) means d(n)/log₂n→∞ as n→∞; it imposes no upper bound such as d=n^{o(1)}. An explicit vector input has nd coordinates, whose bit lengths also affect its size. In an oracle model, evaluating a distance is instead an allowed query; in a distance-matrix model, Θ(n²) distances are part of the input. These representations cannot share an unexplained n-only running-time convention. Standard deterministic SETH says that for every η>0 there is an integer clause width w such that satisfiability of w-CNF formulas on N Boolean variables cannot be decided by a deterministic algorithm in O(2^{(1−η)N}L^{O(1)}) time, where L is the formula encoding length. Each clause has at most w literals. Ruling out bounded-error randomized SAT algorithms is a stronger randomized SETH variant; deterministic SETH alone is not automatically a hardness assumption against all randomized geometric algorithms. A factor of 2−γ, γ>0, or 2−o(1) strictly below 2 does not equal the closed guarantee ≤2OPT. In particular, a promise that OPT is 1 in one case and all distances are 2 in the other cannot by itself distinguish those cases from an arbitrary factor-two output: a distance-2 pair can be allowed in both.
cards.answer_criterion: First recover an intended metric family and its finite input representation, dimension and bit-length regime, cost model, quantifier over metrics, and algorithm/hypothesis randomness convention. Within that specification, establish the requested SETH implication for some constant ε>0 or refute that conditional statement. A result only below approximation factor 2, a lower bound forced by reading a larger input, a bichromatic theorem, or a barrier for one reduction construction does not settle the intended question. These remaining modeling choices are not yet certified.

context_blocks.title: The endpoint is the substantive target
context_blocks.text: The 2018 ℓ∞ theorem gives conditional near-quadratic hardness for approximation ratios strictly below 2. Its distance-1 versus distance-2 promise does not exclude a guarantee that permits equality at factor 2. The 2019 source therefore explicitly asks again about factor exactly 2.

context_blocks.title: Exact and small-factor hardness is already known
context_blocks.text: The 2019 paper proves strong exact Closest Pair hardness and hardness for factors 1+δ in several ℓ_p metrics. Neither statement reaches the requested factor-two endpoint with a superlinear lower bound.

context_blocks.title: A construction barrier is not an algorithm or an impossibility theorem
context_blocks.text: The earlier source explains how the triangle inequality limits certain simple geometric reductions. This observation does not prove that a SETH reduction at factor 2 is impossible, nor does it supply a fast factor-two algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Later diameter reductions address another conditional question
context_blocks.text: The 2023 paper relates subquadratic roundtrip-diameter approximation to approximate ℓ∞ Closest Pair. Its result is not stated as a SETH-based factor-two Closest Pair lower bound and does not supply the missing model choices here.

cards.context:
The 2018 ℓ∞ theorem gives conditional near-quadratic hardness for approximation ratios strictly below 2. Its distance-1 versus distance-2 promise does not exclude a guarantee that permits equality at factor 2. The 2019 source therefore explicitly asks again about factor exactly 2.

The 2019 paper proves strong exact Closest Pair hardness and hardness for factors 1+δ in several ℓ_p metrics. Neither statement reaches the requested factor-two endpoint with a superlinear lower bound.

The earlier source explains how the triangle inequality limits certain simple geometric reductions. This observation does not prove that a SETH reduction at factor 2 is impossible, nor does it supply a fast factor-two algorithm.

The 2023 paper relates subquadratic roundtrip-diameter approximation to approximate ℓ∞ Closest Pair. Its result is not stated as a SETH-based factor-two Closest Pair lower bound and does not supply the missing model choices here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
